sections.heading: The mistake
sections.content: When he joined Slack as its first PM, Berger didn’t ask what success looked like or what the team expected. Overconfidently, he guessed what the job required rather than aligning with the team, which wanted him to come in humbly and earn its trust. He also didn’t articulate his basic goals: doing a good job and having a good relationship with the CEO. He said he wasn’t listening to feedback or the “no’s” indicating his approach wasn’t working.

sections.heading: How it led to unhappiness and firing
sections.content: Berger said he kept what he really wanted and felt to himself because he was scared, and couldn’t accept the negative feedback. Instead, he blamed the CEO. He described the result as a year of suffering and being “out of integrity” with himself; his retrospective lesson was that he hadn’t articulated or asked for what he wanted, or listened to the responses. He was fired six weeks into the job, later returned to product after proposing a plan, and ultimately said he lasted only a year at Slack.

sections.content: Berger said he went into Slack without clarifying expectations or what success looked like, made his own guess, and did not articulate even basic goals: doing a good job and having a good relationship with the CEO. After being reinstated following an initial firing, he spent a year afraid to voice what he wanted, despite one-on-ones with the CEO. He said he also failed to listen to repeated negative signals that his work was not working; instead, he blamed the CEO. In retrospect, he called it ineffective asking: he had not articulated or asked for what he wanted, and had not listened to the “no’s” in response to his non-ask. He said that left him unhappy and out of integrity with himself, and contributed to his eventual firing.
